subject: vocab
title: Vocabulary Builder — Grade 6 Word Power (ELA.6.V)
intro: Vocabulary is one of the biggest parts of the FAST reading test. This builder grows your word power the way the test checks it — figuring out words from context, breaking words into prefixes, suffixes, and roots, telling apart shades of meaning, and mastering the academic words that show up in school texts.

lessons.title: Using Context Clues
lessons.teach:
When you meet a word you don't know, the words AROUND it are clues to its meaning. This is the #1 vocabulary skill on the FAST, because the test almost always asks what a word means "as used in" a sentence.

Four kinds of context clues:
1) DEFINITION clue — the sentence tells you straight out: "A glacier, a huge sheet of slow-moving ice, covered the valley."
2) SYNONYM clue — a nearby word means the same: "The path was treacherous, or dangerous, after the rain."
3) ANTONYM/CONTRAST clue — a nearby word means the opposite, often after but, unlike, however: "Unlike his timid sister, Marcus was bold." (bold = opposite of timid)
4) EXAMPLE clue — examples show the meaning: "Citrus fruits, such as oranges, lemons, and limes, are full of vitamin C."

How to do it: read the WHOLE sentence (and the one before/after), find the clue, then put a simpler word in place of the hard word and check that it still makes sense.

lessons.title: Prefixes
lessons.teach:
A PREFIX is a word part added to the FRONT of a base word to change its meaning. Knowing common prefixes lets you unlock words you have never seen.

Most useful Grade 6 prefixes:
- un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, non- = NOT (unhappy, invisible, impossible, illegal, nonfiction)
- re- = again or back (rebuild, return)
- pre- = before (preview, prehistoric)
- mis- = wrongly (misread, misbehave)
- dis- = not or opposite of (disagree, disappear)
- sub- = under (submarine, subway)
- super- = above/over (superhuman, supermarket)
- inter- = between (interact, international)
- trans- = across (transport, translate)
- anti- = against (antifreeze)

How to do it: cover the prefix, read the base word, then add the prefix meaning. "Pre + view" = view before = a look before the real thing.

lessons.title: Suffixes
lessons.teach:
A SUFFIX is a word part added to the END of a base word. Suffixes often change the word's job (its part of speech) and add meaning.

Most useful Grade 6 suffixes:
- -less = without (fearless, hopeless)
- -ful = full of (joyful, careful)
- -able / -ible = able to be (readable, reversible)
- -er / -or = a person who (teacher, actor)
- -ist = a person who (artist, scientist)
- -ish = somewhat / like (childish, reddish)
- -ous = full of (dangerous, famous)
- -ment = the act or result of (movement, agreement)
- -tion / -sion = the act or state of (action, decision)
- -ly = in a way (quickly, happily) — makes an adverb

How to do it: find the base word, then add the suffix meaning. "Fear + less" = without fear. Watch spelling changes: happy + ness = happiness (y to i).

lessons.title: Greek & Latin Roots
lessons.teach:
A ROOT is the core part that carries a word's main meaning. Many English words are built on Greek and Latin roots, so learning a few roots unlocks dozens of words.

High-value roots for Grade 6:
- bio = life (biology, biography)
- graph / gram = write or draw (autograph, telegram, paragraph)
- tele = far / distant (telephone, television, telescope)
- port = carry (transport, portable, import)
- scrib / script = write (scribble, manuscript, describe)
- spect = look / see (inspect, spectator, telescope)
- struct = build (construct, structure, destruction)
- aud = hear (audience, audio, audible)
- vis / vid = see (vision, video, visible)
- dict = say / speak (dictionary, predict, dictate)
- geo = earth (geography, geology)
- meter = measure (thermometer, perimeter)

How to do it: spot the root, recall its meaning, and combine it with the prefix/suffix. "Tele (far) + scope (look)" = a tool to look far away.

lessons.title: Synonyms & Antonyms
lessons.teach:
A SYNONYM is a word that means the SAME (or nearly the same) as another word. An ANTONYM is a word that means the OPPOSITE.

Synonyms: happy/glad, big/large, fast/quick, smart/clever, brave/courageous, tired/exhausted.
Antonyms: hot/cold, up/down, begin/end, ancient/modern, expand/shrink, generous/stingy.

Why it matters on the test: questions ask "which word means MOST NEARLY the same" (synonym) or "which word means the OPPOSITE." Synonyms can have slightly different strengths — "warm," "hot," and "scorching" are related but not equal — so pick the BEST match for the sentence, not just any related word.

How to do it: say the target word's meaning in your own words, then find the choice that matches it best. For antonyms, find the choice that means the reverse.

lessons.title: Multiple-Meaning Words
lessons.teach:
Many common words have MORE THAN ONE meaning. The FAST tests whether you can pick the meaning that fits THIS sentence — context decides.

Examples:
- bark = the sound a dog makes OR the outer covering of a tree
- bat = a flying animal OR a stick used in baseball
- light = not heavy OR brightness / not dark
- trunk = an elephant's nose OR the storage space of a car OR the main stem of a tree
- current = happening now OR the flow of water/electricity
- left = the opposite of right OR the past tense of leave
- fair = a carnival OR treating people equally OR light-colored

How to do it: read the sentence, decide what is being talked about, then choose the meaning that fits. "Put the suitcase in the trunk" — we are talking about a car, so trunk = car storage.

lessons.title: Connotation & Shades of Meaning
lessons.teach:
DENOTATION is a word's exact dictionary meaning. CONNOTATION is the FEELING or idea a word carries — positive, negative, or neutral. Writers choose words for their connotation, and the FAST asks how a word's connotation shapes meaning, tone, or mood.

Words can share a denotation but feel very different:
- thin (neutral) / slender (positive) / scrawny (negative)
- confident (positive) / proud (neutral) / arrogant (negative)
- curious (positive) / nosy (negative)
- save (positive) / hoard (negative)
- young (neutral) / childish (negative) / youthful (positive)

Shades of meaning = the small differences in strength: warm < hot < scorching; like < love < adore; upset < angry < furious.

How to do it: ask "does this word make the thing sound GOOD, BAD, or neutral?" Then match the feeling the sentence needs. Calling someone "slender" is a compliment; "scrawny" is an insult — same body, different feeling.

lessons.title: Academic Words
lessons.teach:
ACADEMIC WORDS (also called Tier 2 words) are the "school words" that show up across reading, science, and social studies — and all over the FAST questions themselves. Knowing them helps you understand passages AND the test directions.

High-frequency Grade 6 academic words:
- analyze = to study the parts of something closely
- summarize = to retell the main points briefly
- infer = to figure out something not stated directly, using clues
- evaluate = to judge the value or quality of something
- contrast = to show how things are different
- significant = important
- demonstrate = to show clearly
- evidence = facts or details that support an idea
- determine = to decide or figure out
- emphasize = to give special importance to
- relevant = related to the topic
- objective = based on facts, not feelings

How to do it: learn these as everyday tools. When a question says "Which detail BEST supports...," it is asking for EVIDENCE. When it says "analyze the author's word choice," it wants you to study the parts closely.
